cases.title: PDF → Markdown: internal pass rate 45.17% → 89.89%
cases.summary: To use research papers as knowledge, PDF-to-Markdown conversion had to preserve table values and equations. I traced omissions introduced during AI repair and split processing paths by content type and original layout.
cases.problem: Using research papers as service knowledge required Markdown that preserved not only body text but also tables, equations and figures.
cases.diagram:
flowchart TD
 A[Original PDF] --> B[Separate text, tables, equations and figures]
 B --> C[Preserve text context and position]
 B --> D[AI reads original table and equation regions]
 B --> E[Preserve original figures]
 C --> F[Reassemble in original order]
 D --> F
 E --> F
 F --> G{Check markers and missing content}
 G -->|Pass| H[Converted document]
 G -->|Mismatch| I[Keep original content for that region]
cases.diagramCaption: A conceptual view of processing by content type and reassembling at the original positions. This is the current design; experiments did not all use the same path.
cases.result: Split the same papers into 445 evaluation units covering body text, tables, equations and other content, then compared them with the originals. The existing Docling output and improved pipeline output were evaluated with method names hidden.
cases.tradeoff: Internal LLM evaluation of 4 PDFs (30 pages). Minor differences were allowed for text, headings and figures; tables and equations had to match in values, symbols and structure.
experiments: Selective repair and missed errors
Open-source PDF-to-Markdown conversion damaged table row/column relationships and equations. I needed a way to repair errors without processing everything again.

Selected damaged regions for AI repair, then evaluated repaired and untouched regions separately. Of 96 repaired regions, 85 passed, but 107 errors or omissions remained in untouched content. A separate experiment adding OCR comparison raised the pass rate from 80.00% to 97.53%, but also selected 50 correct regions for repair; the sum of processing-stage times was about 12 minutes 35 seconds.
Selecting repair targets missed errors, and extra checks to catch them added cost. I decided to test whether having AI read every original page could avoid this dependence on damage detection.
Table/equation errors and cost in full-page AI conversion
Selective repair missed errors. Adding OCR checks also flagged correct content, increasing evaluation time and cost.

Full AI conversion of 25 research PDFs (415 pages) achieved a 91.92% content-preservation pass rate. However, only 58.84% of tables and equations fully matched in values and structure, and processing every page incurred substantial API usage.

Rather than send all content through the same AI path, I decided to use AI only where needed for body text and give tables and equations inputs that preserved their structure. I looked for fast text extraction with selective AI repair.
Comparing text extraction and adopting AnyDoc
Full-page AI processing still left table/equation errors and required sending all body text to the model. I needed fast text extraction alongside separate table/equation repair.

I found AnyDoc on Threads and, after seeing its GitHub comparison with Docling, tested it on the same 4 PDFs (30 pages).

The recorded Docling run took 134.19s, while AnyDoc text extraction took 1.68s, about 80 times shorter. Docling’s time also included OCR and table analysis. One AnyDoc document had garbled characters because the PDF lacked mappings from character codes to actual characters.

The processing scopes differed, so this was not an 80-fold improvement in complete conversion. Still, AnyDoc was useful for fast text extraction. I kept separate table/equation repair, switched body extraction to AnyDoc, used AI on garbled or misordered pages, and preserved original figures.

cases.title: RAG evidence coverage: 66.25% → 91.25%, with 75% less time after tuning
cases.summary: Jev improved both accuracy and speed when routing user requests to tasks such as questions or edits. I then applied it to RAG evidence selection, increasing coverage from 66.25% to 91.25%, and reduced its added latency by tuning candidates and parallel batches.
cases.problem: To choose appropriate tasks and answer evidence more reliably, I evaluated Jev first for routing and then expanded it to RAG.
cases.diagram:
flowchart TD
 Q[User question] --> S[Collect semantic and keyword search candidates]
 S --> C[Top 300 candidates]
 C --> J[Jev selects evidence in up to 4 parallel batches]
 J --> E{Sufficient evidence?}
 E -->|Yes| A[Pass selected evidence to answer generation]
 E -->|No| N[No evidence]
cases.diagramCaption: The evaluated evidence-selection design. Reference answers were used only for evaluation, never as retrieval or model inputs.
cases.resultTitle: Questions with sufficient evidence: 53/80 → 73/80; total median time 2.251s
cases.result:
On a self-authored golden set of 80 answerable questions, the share with evidence supporting every required fact rose from 66.25% to 91.25%. On a separate 20 unanswerable questions, false evidence returns fell from 20 to 0. The improved selector was still slower than the original, but I chose Jev because accuracy mattered more to the service.

I also tried grouping equivalent expressions: correct answers stayed similar on 76 questions (71 previously, 72 with Jev), while median decision time fell from 8.162s to 0.254s.
metrics: Evidence coverage (LLM evaluation on golden set)
False evidence returns on 20 unanswerable questions
cases.tradeoff: The time reduction compares Jev settings before and after tuning.
experiments: Routing comparison and the decision to try RAG
Some questions were misclassified as document edits, leading to the wrong action. Task types and additional conditions needed to be selected more accurately and quickly.

Applied Jev, a choice-based decision model released on September 14, to routing questions, document edits, document creation and folder organization.

Across 98 requests, correct task types and additional conditions totaled 77 for the existing JSON approach, 63 for GPT-5-nano given the same options, and 81 for Jev. Median decision time improved from 8.967s to 0.658s.
Jev showed promise in both accuracy and speed. I decided to test it on evidence selection, which previous retrieval changes had not solved.
Full-corpus inspection: evidence coverage on all 90 answerable questions

Using the original question for retrieval and increasing semantic-score weight raised top-1 correct retrieval from 50 to 57 out of 110 questions. However, the experiment had some bias and did not establish reliable evidence selection on new questions.

Tested whether Jev could find evidence missed by retrieval. It inspected all 2,020 evidence units in a test Wiki without retrieval filtering and returned at most 8, matching the existing return limit.

In a semantic evaluation allowing paraphrases, coverage on 90 answerable questions rose from 24/90 (26.7%) to 90/90 (100%). It returned no evidence for all 10 unanswerable questions. Median processing time was 1.511s for the original approach and 5.338s for Jev. Jev processed 26 batches of 80, with up to 4 in parallel.

Full-corpus access found the evidence, but inspecting everything per question would increase calls as documents grew. The test also needed better controls for bias. I decided to reduce candidates through retrieval first, rather than use the 90-question result alone to set the deployment scope.
Controlled comparison on 500 candidates: 87.50% coverage

The full-corpus test needed 26 batches per question. Questions were concentrated in certain technical documents and included document titles. The original search inspected only some pages while Jev saw all evidence, confounding judgment quality with access scope. Both candidate count and comparison conditions needed control.

Created 100 new questions from 9 papers without reusing earlier questions: 63 answerable from one paper, 17 requiring two papers, and 20 unanswerable. Questions, reference answers and required facts were fixed before runs.

After deduplication, BGE-M3 and BM25 selected up to 500 candidates once; both methods received identical text and metadata. The original selector could inspect every candidate page, and both methods returned at most 8 untruncated evidence passages. Reference answers were excluded from retrieval and Jev inputs. GPT and Gemini graded independently without seeing method names or competing outputs, and run order alternated.

GPT-graded coverage rose from 53/80 (66.25%) to 70/80 (87.50%); Gemini also showed improvement, from 52/80 to 74/80. False evidence returns on unanswerable questions fell from 20 to 1. Median time including candidate preparation was 0.431s for the original selector and 9.090s for Jev, which processed batches sequentially.

Jev selected better evidence even with matched candidates and return conditions, so I kept retrieval for candidate collection and Jev for final selection. Results on public papers and self-authored questions were not treated as general accuracy. Next I would tune candidate count and batch processing to reduce sequential waiting.
300 candidates and 4 parallel batches to reduce latency

Jev improved evidence selection, but sequential processing of up to 500 candidates raised median preparation-and-selection time to 9.090s versus 0.431s previously. I needed to reduce waiting without losing accuracy.
Reduced the candidate pool to the top 300 and ran up to 4 batches in parallel. Time fell to 2.251s, while questions with all required evidence increased from 70 to 73.

At 2.251s, the tuned approach was still slower than the original 0.431s. I considered fewer candidates and more parallel batches, but rejected further candidate reduction because some required evidence ranked below 250.

I adopted Jev despite the added latency because accuracy was central to the service.

cases.title: Parallel document analysis: 282.11s → 73.89s
cases.summary: Sequential Wiki generation could make large documents slow to process and hurt the user experience. I measured worker scaling and resource use, then set different scaling policies for document analysis and embedding generation.
cases.problem: I tested parallelism separately for document analysis and embedding generation to reduce waiting in the document-to-Wiki pipeline.
cases.diagram:
flowchart TD
 A[Document processing request] --> K[Kafka distributes document jobs]
 K --> W[Multiple workers with per-worker request limits]
 W --> L[Lock writes within the same workspace]
 V[Embedding generation] --> G[Check contention on a shared GPU]
 L --> D[Check time, memory and content preservation]
 G --> D
 D --> R[Choose scaling policy per stage]
cases.diagramCaption: Evaluated scaling separately for Wiki generation and embedding generation.
cases.resultTitle: 73.8% less analysis time for 4 documents, with about 4× memory
cases.result:
With 4 workers and 2 concurrent requests each, analysis time for 4 documents fell by about 73.8%. Memory rose about fourfold, and output quality varied with configuration. Replaying saved AI responses for 100 documents under 3 queue configurations processed all 300 jobs without omissions or failures.

I adopted a maximum of 4 workers: although memory increased about fourfold, I judged that the AI service’s MSA deployment on EKS could distribute the load.
cases.tradeoff: One analysis run per configuration on the same documents. These are not end-to-end timings including storage and post-processing.
experiments: Worker count: analysis time versus memory
Sequential processing left later documents waiting for earlier external AI responses. I needed to measure both speed gains and memory cost from adding workers.

Increasing workers from 1 to 4 for the same 4 documents reduced analysis time from 282.11s to 73.89s. Combined process memory rose from about 352MiB to 1,401MiB. I also checked that writes to the same workspace waited on a lock while different workspaces proceeded in parallel.

Processing another document during API waits helped, but resources grew with worker count. I decided to evaluate document workers separately from concurrent requests within each worker, and tested whether more concurrent requests could help further.
Extra concurrent requests and GPU contention
More workers reduced analysis time, but it still felt slow. It was unclear whether more requests per worker or more embedding processes on the same GPU would help.

With 4 workers, raising concurrent AI requests per worker from 2 to 4 increased time from 73.89s to 95.92s. Running 2 embedding processes on the same GPU also raised each process’s time from about 9.5s to 19–21s.
Analysis waiting on external responses and embeddings sharing a device behaved differently. Higher concurrency did not always improve speed, so I rejected these changes.

cases.category: AI Agent · User-defined Skills · HITL · Prompt injection
cases.title: User-defined Agent Skills with controlled execution
cases.short: Agent Skills: authoring, validation and approval
cases.summary: Built Agent Skills so users could define and reuse recurring document tasks, such as meeting notes. Connected instruction drafting and checks to user review and publication, followed by separate approval for actual changes.
cases.problem: Built a workflow from Skill authoring and publishing to actual document changes, allowing users to define and reuse their own recurring tasks.
cases.diagram:
flowchart TD
 U[User describes a recurring task] --> S[Draft Skill, mask personal data and check prompt injection]
 S --> P[User review and recheck on publication]
 P --> K[Store reusable instructions]
 Q[User requests document work] --> R[Router selects task and conditions]
 K -. Reuse when needed .-> R
 R --> E[Edit while preserving goal and scope]
 R --> F[Plan folder organization and compare with request]
 E --> V[Check format, edit scope, personal data and injection]
 V --> D[Show validated changes and diff]
 F --> D
 D --> A{User approval}
 A -->|Approve| W[Apply edits or organize folders]
 A -->|Cancel| N[Keep originals]
cases.diagramCaption: User-defined instructions and the document workflow that uses them. Executors do not reclassify the task; they validate proposed changes and apply them after user approval.
cases.resultTitle: Reusable tasks and approval workflow; editing passes 94/114 → 104/114
cases.result:
Users can define recurring tasks, publish them as Skills and reuse them. The final instructions are rechecked on publication; actual document changes require a preview and user approval. In a plan–approve–execute check using 6 documents, folder changes occurred only after approval.

Editing quality was evaluated separately on the same 114 drafts from 19 request types. The original implementation passed 94; improved edit-goal and retry inputs passed 98; adding semantic evaluation and rewriting passed 104. Evaluation checked request fulfillment and meaning preservation. Rewriting based on failure reasons was limited to one attempt, and a second failure returned no edit proposal.

AI drafts instructions and edits, code checks permissions and execution scope, and users decide publication and final application.
cases.tradeoff: Normalized average editing-evaluation time increased from 11.11s to 18.92s. I accepted the latency while limiting rewrites.

links.label: The two sides of LLM evaluation for reliability (Korean)

designSteps.title: Authoring and publishing user-defined instructions
designSteps.problem: Recurring tasks such as meeting notes vary by user; developers cannot prebuild every workflow.
designSteps.judgment: Let users define and reuse natural-language instructions instead of adding each workflow as a feature. Treat AI-generated instructions as proposals until users review them.
designSteps.implementation: Turned natural-language requests into reusable Markdown Skills. Users review and edit drafts; the Skill and version are stored on final publication.
designSteps.verification: Neither Skills nor temporary drafts persist in the DB before publication. Published instructions can be reused in later tasks.

designSteps.title: Checking instructions for permission and approval bypasses
designSteps.problem: User instructions and reference documents could contain personal data or directions to bypass permissions and approval. Such intent can be phrased many ways, and users can edit drafts after review.
designSteps.judgment: Use code for explicit risk and permission checks, and an LLM to detect rephrased bypass intent. Do not allow publication based only on an earlier check after users edit the content.
designSteps.implementation: Applied rule checks to input and reference documents. The server verified that risky phrases reported by the LLM existed in the source. After checking access and original documents, it sent only necessary structure to the model. Publication reran checks on the final content. Risky phrases were not silently deleted; only user-requested regeneration removed them and rechecked the result.
designSteps.verification: Showed blocked input and the problematic location to users, letting them edit it themselves or request regeneration.

designSteps.title: Previewing changes and applying them after approval
designSteps.problem: Publishing a reviewed Skill does not approve every later document change. Users still need to inspect the target documents and proposed modifications.
designSteps.judgment: Separate instruction publication from approval of actual changes. Keep task classification in the router and execution in the executor, while letting users inspect what will change.
designSteps.implementation: Displayed before/after diffs for edits and a folder-and-document move plan for organization. Code checked output format and edit scope; only approved changes were executed.
designSteps.verification: With 6 documents, the plan–approve–execute check made no changes before approval. After approval, it created 3 topic folders and moved the documents.

cases.title: Drug data pipeline: $200 estimated → $11.18 spent
cases.summary: Built a data preparation pipeline to rewrite difficult drug information in plain language. Merged exact duplicates and then equivalent sentences, filled the missing 5% using ingredient-specific precautions, and converted unique text once before mapping it back to each drug. Actual API spending was $11.18.
cases.problem: Built a feature to rewrite about 44,000 drug records into explanations users could understand.
cases.diagram:
flowchart TD
 A[Original drug text: 1GB] --> B[Split into sentence blocks]
 B --> C[Merge exact duplicate sentences]
 C --> D[Merge equivalent sentences, preserving numbers]
 B --> M[Keep drug ID to block ID mappings]
 D --> U[Deduplicated conversion input: 326MB]
 U --> E[Find missing information: about 5%]
 E --> F[Clean and fill precautions by ingredient]
 F --> G[Convert unique sentences with GPT Batch API]
 G --> R[Map converted text back to each drug]
 M --> R
cases.diagramCaption: Removed exact and semantic duplicates separately, filled missing information by ingredient, and mapped converted text back to each drug.
cases.result: Completed conversion for $11.18 in actual API spending versus about $200 estimated for all original text. Removed exact and semantic duplicates, then filled the missing 5% with cleaned ingredient-specific precautions. Reusing converted unique sentences kept the feature within budget without reducing the set of drugs covered.
cases.tradeoff: About $200 was the upfront estimate; $11.18 was actual spending. Labor for 7 days of preprocessing is excluded.

image.alt: Output showing drug text split into indexed blocks with drug ID to block ID mappings
image.caption: Processing output preserving unique sentence blocks and their links to each drug.

experiments: Removing exact duplicate sentences
Converting about 44,000 records totaling 1GB was estimated to cost about $200 in API usage. I needed to cover all drugs within budget.

Examined 100 records and found about 70% duplicate content. Used this sample and a work plan to secure 7 days for preprocessing. Split text into sentence blocks, merged exact matches and preserved links from each drug to its blocks.
Convert repeated sentences once and reuse them rather than cover fewer drugs. Since non-identical duplicates remained, the next step was to identify equivalent sentences with different wording.
Merging semantically equivalent sentences
Exact deduplication left sentences that differed only in endings or phrasing. I needed to avoid repeated conversion while preserving dosage and numeric differences.

Normalized sentence endings and compared similarity to group equivalent sentences. Preserved drug-to-block mappings, handled dosages and numbers separately, and manually checked samples. Exact and semantic deduplication reduced input from 1GB to 326MB.
Reuse equivalent explanations while preserving drug-specific facts and numbers, rather than merge solely on string similarity. Next I checked missing information instead of stopping at deduplication.
Filling the missing 5% with ingredient-specific precautions
About 5% of information was missing after earlier processing, leaving gaps in descriptions for the full target set.
Inspected missing entries and noticed that drugs with the same ingredient shared precautions. Collected and cleaned data for the missing ingredients, then processed it to fill the gaps.
Fill gaps by ingredient instead of excluding records. Shared ingredient precautions maintained coverage without repeatedly processing each drug.
GPT Batch API conversion and mapping results back to drugs
Deduplication reduced input, but I still needed to minimize model costs.

The work did not require immediate responses during service use, so batch waiting was acceptable. Converted unique sentences with GPT Batch API, then reused the preserved drug-to-block mappings to attach results to each drug. Actual API spending was $11.18 versus about $200 estimated for all original text.
Combined deduplication, ingredient-level gap filling and batch conversion to deliver the feature without reducing drug coverage.

cases.title: Medication chatbot: keeping health profiles out of external AI inputs
cases.short: Medication chatbot: health profiles kept internal
cases.summary: Built a medication chatbot using RAG and AI orchestration for app integration. Separated symptom-based drug discovery from health-profile decisions, using the model for language understanding and code to control sensitive profile use.
cases.problem: Built a chatbot that finds drug information from natural-language symptoms and personalizes it using health profiles.
cases.diagram:
flowchart TD
 S[Natural-language symptoms] --> V[Weaviate: semantic search of indications]
 P[Pregnancy, medications and underlying conditions] --> T[Internal tool: profile decisions]
 V --> R[Personalized information]
 T --> R
 B[External LLM input boundary] -.-> X[Exclude these profile fields]
 classDef accent fill:#e5edff,stroke:#4164c8,color:#142b60;
 class T,B,X accent;
cases.diagramCaption: A conceptual view of responsibilities and data boundaries, not the exact call sequence or a guarantee against every form of data leakage.
cases.resultTitle: Separating symptom search from internal health-profile decisions
cases.result: Enabled natural-language drug discovery while excluding pregnancy status, current medications and underlying conditions from external LLM inputs. Explicitly separated information sent to AI from information evaluated by internal code.
cases.tradeoff: Profile-rule changes require code updates. I prioritized keeping those personal data fields out of external AI inputs and retained profile decisions in internal code.

designSteps.title: Semantic search connecting symptoms to drug indications
designSteps.problem: Everyday symptom descriptions and drug indications use different words for the same meaning. Related information needed to be found without exact keyword matches.
designSteps.judgment: Use semantic search to connect symptoms and indications, with separate processing paths for the information each question needs.
designSteps.implementation: Stored drug indications in Weaviate for semantic symptom search. Built paths for drug discovery, medication risks and dosage information according to the question.
designSteps.verification: Implemented natural-language symptom search and routing to the appropriate information-processing path.

designSteps.title: Internal health-profile processing, separate from external AI inputs
designSteps.problem: Personalization required pregnancy status, medications and underlying conditions, but sending those profiles to an external LLM risked exposing sensitive information.
designSteps.judgment: Separate language understanding from profile-condition decisions. Keep profile decisions in internal code where inputs and rules can be controlled directly.
designSteps.implementation: Excluded pregnancy, medication and underlying-condition fields from external LLM inputs. Connected internal profile decisions to symptom search results to provide personalized information.
designSteps.verification: Separated processing paths so those health-profile fields stayed out of external LLM inputs while remaining available for internal personalization.
